results.title: long-term dependencies. Including this and our new perspective, we highlight two critical issues of high recency bias. The first is that a recommendation system with high recency bias seriously lacks serendipity, which is one of the major requirements a fine recommendation system ought to satisfy, as it repeatedly suggests items similar to only those the user recently interacted with. This monotony can quickly bore out user, and further lead to user disengagement. Second, high recency bias means the recommendation system fails to model the entire session into mining user preference, which was the primary goal of sequential recommendation system, and pigeonhole into only users most recent interests, as mentioned in [21]. Still, we lack an universal method to measure this recency bias in existing sequential recommendation models. [21] does measure recency bias, but this is only demonstrated in a reinforcement based setting, not universally applicable to many existing sequential recommendation models, also resulting in the absence of measurement experimental results of recency bias of existing models.

item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports perturbing interaction histories to measure recommendation dependence. Oh and Cho’s [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduces a recency-bias metric and reports that excessive recency emphasis harms performance across their evaluated models. Scarcelli et al.’s [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal history changes that alter recommendations using genetic algorithms, evaluating targeted and untargeted counterfactuals across three datasets and three models. A [2026 temporal-attribution study](https://jidmis.org/index.php/jidmis/article/view/2525) evaluates deletion faithfulness, counterfactual stability, sufficiency, and masking-versus-shuffling consistency; its findings show architecture-dependent reliance on recent versus broader history.\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: on unchanged training-history prefixes, remove equal numbers of recent interactions, interactions representing repeated interests, and isolated interactions; compare each intervention against multiple length-matched random deletions. Define repeated interests using recurring item IDs where available or explicit title/description similarity, without assuming unavailable categories. Measure original top-item rank displacement, score-margin changes, and top-10 overlap using identical candidate sets and eligibility masks. Compare deletion with position-preserving masking and order shuffling to distinguish content dependence from sequence-length and positional effects. Stratify by history length and recurrence. These are proposed controls, rather than an established protocol from the cited papers: deletion sensitivity demonstrates model dependence, but cannot alone establish causal user preference or temporal shortcut learning. Use macro validation HR@10 to assess whether changes motivated by these probes improve the benchmark."}
